notes:
Here are notes on Matthew 13:30–58. A few things to know first:

- **Gaps:** I found nothing on bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org, nothing on v. 58 from a Pentecostal or Word of Faith source, and nothing from an Anglican, Methodist or Lutheran source on Jesus' brothers. Those parts are left out.
- **The big Protestant split** is over vv. 31–33 (is the mustard seed and leaven about good growth or about corruption?) and v. 44 (who finds the treasure?).
- **Pages with partial coverage:** Some pages I read in full have no citation tags; for those I give just the URL. The enduringword page was cut off around v. 24 when I opened it, so the Guzik notes for v. 30 onward come only from the search-result snippet. Matthew Henry's full text also stopped before v. 34, so after that I only have his chapter outline and snippets.

---

**v. 30 – Letting the wheat and weeds grow together**
- Guzik: the farmer decided to sort it out at harvest time. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-13/
- Matthew Henry's outline: the weeds parable and the net parable (vv. 47–50) show that the gospel church will be a mix of good and bad until the final separation on Judgment Day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/matthew/13.htm
- *Where views differ (what is the "field"?):* Constable quotes the view that the parable "is not a description of the world, but of that which professes to be the kingdom [i.e., Christendom]." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/matthew-13.html. Calvin, writing on the net (v. 47), applies the lesson to the Church: it is a mixture of good and bad that must be patiently endured till *the end of the word*. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-13.html

**vv. 31–32 – The mustard seed**
- *Traditional reading (growth):* Jamieson, Fausset & Brown say the mustard seed and the leaven share one theme, THE GROWTH OF THE KINGDOM FROM THE SMALLEST BEGINNINGS TO ULTIMATE UNIVERSALITY. Following Trench, they suggest the birds stand for the shelter and rest the kingdom will give the nations. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Mat/Mat_013.cfm
- Barclay: Jesus is telling disciples not to be discouraged, because each one is a small beginning from which the Kingdom grows until the kingdoms of the earth finally become the Kingdom of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/matthew-13.html
- *Dissenting reading (corruption):* David Guzik (enduringword) admits that most see this as the church growing. But he reads it as another description of *corruption* in the kingdom community. He says it describes the church after the Roman Empire became Christian, when it grew abnormally large in influence and dominion, and was a nest for much corruption. He quotes G. Campbell Morgan that the birds stand for corrupting elements. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-13/
- Preceptaustin warns against reading the parable as a promise that preaching will win the whole world. It says the parables of the sower and the weeds demonstrate that the church and its rule will be neither universal nor perfect. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-13-commentary

**v. 33 – The leaven**
- *Traditional reading (good influence):* Ellicott says the leaven pictures the Church's effect on the world. Unlike the mustard seed's outward growth through missions, Here the working is from within. https://biblehub.com/matthew/13-33.htm
- Gill notes that "leaven" is negative everywhere else in Scripture, yet here it seems to be taken in a good sense, and the Gospel to be compared unto it. He also mentions a late ingenious interpretation in which the leaven is the spread of error and the woman is the "whore of Rome." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/13-33.html
- Spurgeon (Baptist) rejects the "evil" reading. The parable opens like the others, and there is not a word to warn us that the theme is changed, and that our Lord is not now speaking of the kingdom itself, but of evil in the kingdom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-13-commentary-spurgeon
- Coffman agrees. If the leaven were evil, the parable would predict the complete, final, and total corruption of the church itself, which cannot be. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/13-33.html
- GotQuestions: here leaven is not used as a symbol of evil; rather, leaven is a symbol of the kingdom, which will gradually and secretly permeate society. https://www.gotquestions.org/leaven-in-the-Bible.html
- *Dissenting reading:* Guzik says leaven is consistently used as a picture of sin and corruption. He argues the scene certainly isn't a picture of the church gradually influencing the whole world for *good*. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-13/
- *A caution on the optimistic reading:* the Pulpit Commentary says the parable promises the kingdom will finally succeed. But it is unfair to so press the parable as to deduce from it that the world as such will continue to be gradually and continuously improved up to the Lord's return. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/13-33.htm
- *Church Fathers:* a Bible Hub article says most early fathers—Origen, Athanasius, Chrysostom—see leaven as the gospel's quiet, irreversible penetration of society and the individual heart. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_leaven_parable_in_Matthew.htm

**vv. 34–35 – Why Jesus taught in parables**
- Matthew Henry: Jesus used parables because the time was not yet come for the more clear and plain discoveries of the mysteries of the kingdom. The quotation comes from Psalm 78:2, applied to Christ's sermons. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_013.cfm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/matthew/13.htm
- Calvin thinks Jesus kept using parables not so much for the purpose of instruction, as to keep the attention of his hearers awake till a more convenient time. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-13.html
- Guzik: the church itself was among the things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-13/

**vv. 36–39 – The weeds explained**
- Guzik: Jesus spelled out what each figure means, and here In the parable of the soils, the seed represented the Word of God; here it represents true believers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-13/
- Barclay translates "weeds" as "darnel." He notes that in codified Roman law, sowing bad seed in an enemy's field is forbidden and its punishment laid down. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/matthew-13.html

**vv. 40–42 – Judgment at the end of the age**
- Spurgeon: Not only the outwardly wicked, but the false pretenders, the mock wheat, shall be removed. This will be the purging not of the church, but of the kingdom, which at that time will include the whole field of the world. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-13-commentary-spurgeon
- Guzik: Jesus teaches that there are two different paths and eternal destinies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-13/

**v. 43 – The righteous will shine**
- Matthew Henry finds the verse "gloriously represented." Heaven is a granary where the wheat is not only separated from the weeds but sifted from the chaff of their own corruptions. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_013.cfm

**v. 44 – The hidden treasure**
- *Traditional reading (the disciple gives up all):* Calvin says the treasure and pearl teach believers to put the Kingdom ahead of the whole world and deny themselves to gain it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-13.html. In his verse note, the point is that none are qualified for receiving the grace of the Gospel but those who disregard all other desires. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/13-44.html
- GotQuestions: The treasure and the pearl represent Jesus Christ and the salvation He offers. https://www.gotquestions.org/parable-treasure-pearl.html. Gill instead says the treasure is the Gospel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/13-44.html
- Carson (quoted by Guzik): finding treasure like this would be rare, so the extravagance of the parable dramatizes the supreme importance of the kingdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-13/
- *Was the man dishonest?* Barnes says Christ does not intend to vindicate his conduct. He merely states the way in which people do "actually" manage to obtain wealth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/13-44.html
- *Where views differ (who is the buyer?):*
  - **Lutheran (1517.org):** making ourselves the seekers and Jesus the prize gets it backwards. We are the hidden treasure and the pearl of great value. Jesus is the man in the field and the searching merchant. He gives everything, including his life, so that he can redeem us from sin, death, and the devil. https://www.1517.org/articles/understanding-jesus-parables
  - **Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel)** takes the same direction: Jesus purchased the world in order that He might take the bride out of it, His church, the treasure. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/13-44.html
  - **Guzik:** these two parables speak of how highly the King values the people of His kingdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-13/
  - **Constable disagrees.** Of the view that the buyer is Jesus paying with His life, he writes: This seems unlikely to me since in all these parables the focus seems to be on the disciples more than on Jesus. They should pay the price. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/13-44.html
  - **Arnot tries to hold both together.** Salvation is in one sense a purchase and in another a free gift bestowed by God for Christ's sake; this parable only shows the first side. https://biblehub.com/library/arnot/the_parables_of_our_lord/v_the_hidden_treasure.htm
- *Dispensational view:* Constable notes that several dispensational interpreters believe the treasure in the field or land represents Israel and that the pearl, taken from the sea, represents the Gentiles. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/13-45.html

**vv. 45–46 – The pearl**
- Coffman contrasts the two parables: the treasure was found without looking, but the pearl its discovery followed a long and diligent search for it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/13-44.html
- Barclay: since a pearl was the loveliest possession, the Kingdom of Heaven is the loveliest thing in the world. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/13-44.html
- Gill offers the "Christ is the merchant" reading as possible: This parable may be understood of Christ's seeking, finding, and purchasing his elect. He prefers to see a seeker who finds the Gospel. Chuck Smith: Now Jesus isn't the pearl of great price, that you have to sell everything and buy Him. The gift of Jesus is by free grace to you. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/13-45.html

**vv. 47–50 – The net**
- Calvin: nothing new here. The parable confirms that the Church of God, so long as it exists in the world, is a mixture of the good with the bad. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-13.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says the net parable was meant to save them from presumption. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/13-44.html
- Guzik: the world will remain divided right up until the end, and the Church will not reform the world, ushering in the kingdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-13/
- Constable: the point was the sorting out of righteous and wicked individuals that will happen then. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/matthew-13.html

**vv. 51–52 – The scribe with new and old treasures**
- Matthew Henry calls this the parable of the good householder. It tells the disciples to use what they have learned for the good of others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/matthew/13.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary: when the disciples said they understood, he shows them further possibilities. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/13-44.html
- Constable says The final set of parables reveals the disciples' dual responsibilities. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/matthew-13.html
- Barclay (this note appears to be about v. 52): Jesus never meant converts to forget what they knew. They should see his knowledge in a new light and use it in a new service. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/13-44.html

**vv. 53–54 – Back in Nazareth**
- Chrysostom: Jesus moved on because He wanted to sow the word everywhere. His "own country" here means Nazareth. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200148.htm
- Chrysostom: they should have been amazed, but they on the contrary hold Him cheap, because of him who seemed to be His father. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200148.htm

**vv. 55–56 – "The carpenter's son" and His brothers and sisters**
- Chrysostom: humble parents should have made His wisdom more astonishing, since it showed it was not of man's care, but of God's grace. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200148.htm. They found no fault with His teaching but take refuge in the meanness of His race. https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf110/npnf110.iii.XLVIII.html
- The Catholic Encyclopedia concludes from the townspeople's dismissive words that Mary belonged to the lower social order of townspeople. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/15464b.htm?vm=r
- *Who were the "brothers"?*
  - **Evangelical (GotQuestions):** Mary was a virgin when Jesus was born, but the Bible does not teach that she remained a virgin for the rest of her life. Matthew names Jesus' four half-brothers. https://www.gotquestions.org/virgin-Mary.html. GotQuestions grants that Catholics are right that the Greek words can mean "relatives," but says the plain meaning here is literal family. https://www.gotquestions.org/perpetual-virginity-Mary.html
  - **Bible Hub:** the risen Christ transformed their unbelief, and James and Judas went on to write the New Testament letters that bear their names. https://biblehub.com/matthew/13-55.htm
  - **Catholic (catholic.com):** the claim that *adelphos* can only mean a full sibling is wrong. at least two of the men mentioned in Matthew 13 were definitely not siblings of Jesus; they were cousins. https://www.catholic.com/qa/does-the-use-of-this-greek-word-for-sibling-indicate-that-jesus-had-brothers
  - Another catholic.com speaker favours the "Epiphanian" view (stepbrothers, Joseph's children by an earlier marriage), but adds you're still allowed to believe in St. Jerome's view that the brothers of the Lord are cousins. https://www.catholic.com/audio/cot/answering-objections-to-marys-perpetual-virginity
  - **Patristic debate (Bible Hub):** Helvidius (4th c.) argued for Mary's subsequent children, prompting Jerome's rebuttal. https://biblehub.com/q/Does_Matt_13_55_suggest_Jesus_had_siblings.htm

**v. 57 – A prophet without honour**
- Chrysostom points to Jesus' gentleness: He does not insult them. He thinks the words "in his own house" quietly refer to Jesus' own brothers. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200148.htm

**v. 58 – Few miracles because of unbelief**
- Matthew Henry: if mighty works be not wrought in us, it is not for want of power or grace in Christ, but for want of faith in us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/matthew/13.htm
- Chrysostom: Jesus held back miracles not from lack of power. He cared about their good rather than showing Himself, and did not want to deepen their guilt. He still did a few so they could not say they would have believed if they had seen miracles. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200148.htm
